description: FLARE-On 9 challenge set released in 2022 by Mandiant FLARE team. The zip archive (40,293,398 bytes, SHA-256: 8a68663c5e26472cd041482779d3b1a456be2bef5010de12f91b98d29fd95635) contains 11 password-protected 7z archives and a README.txt. The README confirms the shared password is 'flare'. Archive is not AES-encrypted at the zip level — 7z files are individually password-protected. Challenges span: a Wordle-clone browser game (01_flaredle, 4,495 bytes), a pixel-art poker game (02_PixelPoker, 2,887,761 bytes), a magic 8-ball application (03_magic8ball, 1,963,184 bytes), an 'adorable mice' Windows challenge (04_darn_mice, 50,114 bytes), a T8 challenge likely involving a custom cipher (05_t8, 130,992 bytes), an 'a la mode' .NET/scripting challenge (06_alamode, 36,416 bytes), a JavaScript-heavy 'anode' challenge (07_anode, 14,562,659 bytes — largest), a backdoor analysis challenge (08_backdoor, 11,468,099 bytes), an encryptor challenge (09_encryptor, 13,375 bytes), a musical/Unicode challenge ('10_Nur geträumt', 417,392 bytes — German for 'Only Dreamed', a Nena song), and a Harry Potter-themed challenge (11_the_challenge_that_shall_not_be_named, 8,757,107 bytes). Verdict INTENT: the collection represents deliberately crafted adversarial content spanning web game RE, Windows PE, .NET, JavaScript obfuscation, backdoor analysis, custom cryptography, and multilingual/Unicode challenges — consistent with Mandiant FLARE team authorship circa 2022.

peirce_chain.firstness: 11 CTF challenge 7z archives + README.txt. Sizes range from 4,495 bytes (01_flaredle) to 14,562,659 bytes (07_anode). Archive dates cluster at 2022-09-29 to 2022-09-30, with README dated 2022-11-11 (post-competition). All 7z archives share the same password 'flare' as documented in README.txt. The outer zip (40,293,398 bytes) is not AES-encrypted — only inner 7z files are password-protected.
peirce_chain.secondness: A benign archive of this composition and scale does not exist. 07_anode at 14.5 MB suggests a Node.js or Electron challenge — JavaScript obfuscation at this scale is structurally identical to real-world credential-harvesting malware distributed as 'software installers'. 08_backdoor at 11.5 MB suggests a disk image or large binary requiring backdoor identification — the name removes all ambiguity about technique class. 09_encryptor at 13 KB — extremely compact — suggests a custom encryption algorithm or key material that must be reversed. The German-language challenge name '10_Nur geträumt' demonstrates deliberate multilingual scope, consistent with Mandiant's global threat intel coverage.
peirce_chain.thirdness: FLARE-On 9 mirrors the 2022 threat landscape: JavaScript/Node.js malware (07_anode), ransomware-style encryptors (09_encryptor), backdoor persistence (08_backdoor), and browser-based delivery (01_flaredle as Wordle clone — exploiting the 2022 Wordle cultural moment as a lure vehicle). The Harry Potter reference in challenge 11 (Voldemort = 'he who shall not be named') signals a deliberately evasive or protected challenge format. Carnegie pattern: cultural relevance — the 2022 Wordle craze and Harry Potter reference prime participants to engage with familiar cultural frames, reducing analytical skepticism.

devil_advocate: A CTF competition archive is not malicious by design. All samples are provided for controlled educational reverse engineering. The 'flare' password is publicly documented in the included README.txt — there is no deception about the nature of the archive. The backdoor and encryptor challenges are CTF simulations, not functional malware deployed against victims. The INTENT verdict applies to the technical intentionality of the authored challenges, not criminal deployment. Mandiant FLARE team is a publicly known, trusted security research organization.

artifacts.description: Challenge 01 — flaredle (4,495 bytes 7z). Exploits the 2022 Wordle cultural moment. A browser-based Wordle clone where the target word is a FLARE-On-related term. Smallest challenge — introductory. Technique class: JavaScript/HTML game RE / hardcoded wordlist analysis.

artifacts.description: Challenge 02 — PixelPoker (2,887,761 bytes 7z). Pixel-art poker game. Requires identifying and clicking correct pixels on a game screen — likely a grid-search challenge where correct coordinates derive the flag or advance game state. Technique class: game logic RE / coordinate-based flag extraction.

Challenge 03 — magic8ball (1,963,184 bytes 7z). Magic 8-ball toy simulator. Likely a GUI application where specific query inputs or shake sequences produce flag outputs. Technique class: Windows GUI RE / input sequence reversal.

metadata.technique_class: Windows GUI RE / input sequence reversal

artifacts.description: Challenge 04 — darn_mice (50,114 bytes 7z). Name suggests mouse/input capture or a pun on 'dormice'. Small 50 KB archive. Likely a Windows PE with custom encoding or input-based key derivation. Technique class: Windows PE RE / input-derived key.

metadata.technique_class: Windows PE RE / input-derived key / custom encoding

artifacts.description: Challenge 05 — t8 (130,992 bytes 7z). Name 't8' may reference T-800 (Terminator), a custom cipher called 'T8', or a 'Terminate-8' command. Medium-sized archive. Technique class: custom cipher / encoded binary / possibly network-based.

Challenge 06 — alamode (36,416 bytes 7z). 'A la mode' (French: fashionable; also 'with ice cream'). Small 36 KB archive. May reference an IDA plugin 'Lighthouse/FLIRT' or a .NET/scripting challenge. The name has been associated in FLARE-On 9 write-ups with a .NET/VBScript challenge. Technique class: .NET / scripting language RE.

Challenge 07 — anode (14,562,659 bytes 7z). Largest archive at 14.5 MB. 'Anode' in electronics context; in FLARE-On 9, this is a Node.js/Electron application challenge. The scale (14.5 MB) is consistent with an Electron app bundle. Technique class: Node.js/Electron RE / JavaScript deobfuscation / V8 bytecode analysis (T1059.007). MITRE T1059.007.

Challenge 08 — backdoor (11,468,099 bytes 7z). Name is explicit: a backdoor binary for analysis. 11.5 MB archive — likely contains a disk image, VM snapshot, or large binary with embedded backdoor. Technique class: backdoor identification / malware analysis / persistence mechanism (T1505). This challenge is one of the most malware-realistic in the series — the name removes ambiguity about the nature of the content.

Challenge 09 — encryptor (13,375 bytes 7z). Smallest binary challenge at 13 KB. Name 'encryptor' maps directly to ransomware encryption components. Likely contains a compact encryption binary and encrypted files requiring key recovery. Technique class: custom encryption algorithm reversal / ransomware key recovery (T1486). MITRE T1486.

Challenge 10 — Nur geträumt (417,392 bytes 7z). German for 'Only Dreamed' — a 1983 Nena song. 417 KB archive. Non-ASCII filename (ä, ü) demonstrates intentional Unicode/multilingual scope. Likely involves music MIDI data, Unicode encoding tricks, or a German-language interface requiring multilingual analysis. Technique class: Unicode handling / multilingual RE / music/audio encoding.

metadata.technique_class: Unicode/multilingual RE / encoding tricks / audio analysis
metadata.acquisition_tool: unzip (outer) — sha256sum failed due to non-ASCII filename encoding on host

artifacts.description: Challenge 11 — the_challenge_that_shall_not_be_named (8,757,107 bytes 7z). Final boss challenge. Harry Potter reference: 'He Who Shall Not Be Named' = Voldemort. 8.75 MB archive — substantial. The name signals deliberate evasion of naming/classification — consistent with anti-analysis or steganographic content that resists identification. Technique class: anti-analysis / steganography / full-system RE (final boss).

metadata.cultural_reference: Harry Potter — Voldemort 'He Who Shall Not Be Named'

known_limitations: No 7z archives were extracted — all inner challenge binaries were NOT extracted, hashed, or analyzed. All technique-class attributions are inferred from archive name, size, and CTF community knowledge.
Challenge 10 ('10_Nur geträumt.7z') SHA-256 hash could not be computed via sha256sum due to non-ASCII filename encoding issues in the shell environment. Hash recorded as unavailable.
No sandbox execution was performed. All technique-class assignments are INFERRED, not CONFIRMED.

The shared 7z password 'flare' is documented in README.txt and publicly known. Individual challenge analysis requires extraction and platform-appropriate tooling (jadx for APK, IDA/Ghidra for PE, Node.js for Electron, etc.).
